items.q: In what order is a SELECT-FROM-WHERE block conceptually evaluated?
options: FROM (form the product), then WHERE (filter rows), then SELECT (pick columns)
items.explain: Although SELECT is written first, evaluation is FROM → WHERE → SELECT: form the working table, filter rows, then project/derive the surviving columns.

items.q: By default, a SQL SELECT returns a:
options: Multiset (duplicates allowed) — use DISTINCT to remove them
items.explain: SQL relations are multisets; duplicates are kept (this is ALL). DISTINCT forces set semantics by eliminating duplicate rows.

items.q: In a LIKE pattern, what do `%` and `_` match?
options: % = one char, _ = any number of chars
% = any number of chars (incl. zero), _ = exactly one char
items.explain: `%` matches any substring (zero or more characters); `_` matches exactly one character. So `'___'` matches strings of exactly 3 characters.

items.q: Which clause sorts query output, and what is its default direction?
items.explain: ORDER BY sorts the result; ASC (ascending) is the default. Multiple keys are applied left-to-right, the later key breaking ties of the earlier.

items.q: What is required for two queries to be combined with UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT?
options: They must query the same table
They must be union-compatible: same number of columns with compatible types
They must each return one row
items.explain: Set operators need union-compatible inputs: identical column counts and type-compatible columns in matching positions.

items.q: How do UNION and UNION ALL differ?
options: UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps all duplicates
UNION ALL removes duplicates; UNION keeps them
UNION sorts, UNION ALL does not
items.explain: Plain set operators eliminate duplicates. The ALL variants preserve duplicates (and are faster since no de-duplication is needed).

items.q: If a tuple appears 5 times in A and 2 times in B, how many times does it appear in A INTERSECT ALL B and A EXCEPT ALL B?
items.explain: INTERSECT ALL gives min(c1,c2)=min(5,2)=2; EXCEPT ALL gives max(c1−c2,0)=max(5−2,0)=3. (UNION ALL would give 5+2=7.)

items.q: On a MySQL version before 8.0.31, how can `A INTERSECT B` be simulated?
options: With a subquery using IN / EXISTS
items.explain: INTERSECT and EXCEPT arrived in MySQL 8.0.31. Earlier, intersection is written with IN/EXISTS and difference with NOT IN/NOT EXISTS.

items.q: What is the result of the comparison `salary = NULL`?
items.explain: Any comparison involving NULL yields UNKNOWN — even NULL = NULL. That is why = can never test for null; you must use IS NULL.

items.q: A row is kept by a WHERE clause only when the predicate evaluates to:
options: TRUE (rows giving FALSE or UNKNOWN are discarded)
items.explain: WHERE keeps a row only if the predicate is TRUE. Both FALSE and UNKNOWN cause the row to be dropped — so `WHERE salary > 50000` silently excludes NULL salaries.

items.q: In three-valued logic, what is `TRUE AND UNKNOWN`?
items.explain: TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN (the unknown operand decides). By contrast FALSE AND UNKNOWN = FALSE, and TRUE OR UNKNOWN = TRUE.

items.q: For DISTINCT and GROUP BY, how are two NULL values treated?
options: As equal / duplicates of each other
items.explain: Deliberately inconsistent with comparison: for DISTINCT, GROUP BY and UNION, two NULLs are treated as equal, so SELECT DISTINCT collapses them into a single NULL row.

items.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(salary)?
options: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(salary) counts only rows where salary IS NOT NULL
COUNT(*) ignores nulls; COUNT(salary) counts nulls
items.explain: COUNT(*) counts every row including nulls; COUNT(attr) counts non-null values of that attribute. COUNT(DISTINCT attr) counts distinct non-null values.

items.q: How do SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN treat NULL inputs?
options: They return NULL if any value is null
They ignore NULLs (compute over non-null values only)
items.explain: All aggregates except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs. So AVG averages only the non-null values. If a group is entirely NULL, SUM/AVG/MAX/MIN return NULL but COUNT(col) returns 0.

items.q: Why use `WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM instructor)` instead of ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1?
options: It returns ALL instructors tied for the maximum, not just one
items.explain: Comparing to the MAX returns every row that ties for the highest value; ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 would arbitrarily return only one of the tied rows.

items.q: In a GROUP BY query, a column in the SELECT list that is not inside an aggregate must:
options: Appear in the GROUP BY clause
items.explain: Each group yields one row, so every selected non-aggregated column must be a grouping key — otherwise it is ambiguous which value to display.

items.q: Which clause filters GROUPS (and may reference aggregate values)?
items.explain: HAVING is a filter applied after grouping, so it can use aggregates (e.g. HAVING AVG(salary) > 42000). WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates.

items.q: Which lists the correct conceptual evaluation order of a full query?
options: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY
FROM → GROUP BY → WHERE → SELECT → HAVING → ORDER BY
WHERE → FROM → SELECT → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
items.explain: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. This is why a SELECT alias can be used in ORDER BY (runs last) but usually not in WHERE (runs early).

items.q: A NATURAL JOIN matches rows on which columns and keeps how many copies of them?
options: On the primary key; two copies
On all commonly-named columns; one copy each
On explicitly listed columns only; two copies
items.explain: Natural join equates all attributes that share a name in both tables and keeps a single copy of each common column.

items.q: A LEFT OUTER JOIN of A and B returns:
options: All rows of A, with NULLs where B has no match
All rows of B, with NULLs where A has no match
items.explain: LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves every row of the left table; unmatched right-side columns are padded with NULL. (RIGHT keeps all of B; FULL keeps both.)

items.q: MySQL lacks FULL OUTER JOIN. How is it typically emulated?
items.explain: Combine a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN with UNION; UNION (not UNION ALL) removes the duplicated matched rows.

items.q: A CROSS JOIN of relations with |A|=4 and |B|=3 produces how many rows?
items.explain: A cross join is the Cartesian product: |A| × |B| = 4 × 3 = 12 rows, with degree = sum of the two column counts.

items.q: The SQL operator that tests set membership (value present in a subquery's result) is:
items.explain: IN returns TRUE if the value occurs in the set returned by the subquery; NOT IN is its negation.

items.q: `= SOME` (= ANY) is equivalent to which operator?
items.explain: = SOME / = ANY is equivalent to IN. Correspondingly, <> ALL is equivalent to NOT IN.

items.q: `Salary > ALL (SELECT Salary FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno=5)` is equivalent to:
items.explain: > ALL means greater than every value in the set, i.e. greater than the maximum. Likewise > SOME means greater than the minimum.

items.q: A subquery used in the FROM clause must always have:
items.explain: A derived table in FROM must be given an alias so the outer query can reference it as a relation.

items.q: How long does a Common Table Expression (CTE) defined with WITH exist?
options: Only for the duration of the single statement it is part of
items.explain: A CTE is a temporary, named result set that lives only for the one query — unlike a view, which persists in the schema.

items.q: Which is the correct syntax for two CTEs at the same query level?
options: WITH cte1 AS (...) WITH cte2 AS (...)
items.explain: Only one WITH keyword is allowed per level; separate multiple CTEs with commas.

items.q: A recursive CTE consists of which two parts, combined by UNION ALL?
options: An anchor member (base case) and a recursive member that references the CTE
items.explain: The anchor runs once to seed the result; the recursive member repeatedly references the CTE, adding rows until none are new. Used for hierarchies.

items.q: In a recursive CTE, the column data types are determined by:
options: The anchor (non-recursive) member — the recursive part must match
items.explain: Types are fixed by the anchor SELECT; the recursive part must conform. Columns are nullable by default, and mismatches may need an explicit CAST.

items.q: In a CASE expression with multiple WHEN conditions and no matching branch and no ELSE, the result is:
items.explain: Conditions are tested top-down and the first match wins; if none match and there is no ELSE, CASE returns NULL.

items.q: When bucketing scores into grades with CASE (F if <40, C if <60, ...), why must `score < 40` come before `score < 60`?
options: Because the first matching WHEN wins, so the most specific bound must be tested first
items.explain: CASE returns on the first TRUE condition. Testing the lowest bound first ensures a score of 35 hits 'F' rather than falling through to a broader later condition.

items.q: What makes a subquery 'correlated'?
options: It returns more than one row
Its WHERE clause references an attribute of the outer query, so it is re-evaluated per outer row
It appears in the FROM clause
items.explain: A correlated subquery depends on the current outer-query row and is therefore evaluated once for each outer tuple.

items.q: `EXISTS (subquery)` returns TRUE when:
options: The subquery returns at least one row
The subquery returns exactly one row
items.explain: EXISTS is TRUE if the subquery yields one or more rows; NOT EXISTS is TRUE if it yields none. Only existence matters, so the body is usually SELECT *.

items.q: To find employees who work on EVERY project of department 4 (a 'for all'/division query), the standard technique is:
options: Double NOT EXISTS (or NOT EXISTS with EXCEPT)
items.explain: SQL has no universal quantifier, so 'works on all X' is rewritten as 'there is no X the employee does not work on' — double NOT EXISTS, or NOT EXISTS over a set difference.

items.q: 'Employees who have NO dependents' is best written with:
options: A single NOT EXISTS correlated subquery
items.explain: 'No dependents' / 'not any' is a simple single NOT EXISTS. The double-negation pattern is only needed for 'every/all' (division) queries.

items.q: A view is:
options: A copy of the table's data
A virtual table that stores a query, computed from base tables on demand
items.explain: A view stores only a query definition, not data; its rows are derived from the underlying base tables whenever the view is used.

items.q: Which view is NOT updatable through INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE?
options: A view selecting some columns of a single table
A view built on a JOIN of two tables
A view with a simple WHERE filter on one table
A view renaming columns of one table
items.explain: A multi-table (join) view is read-only. Updatable views must be on a single table with no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, joins, or subqueries.

items.q: A key difference between a View and a CTE is:
options: A view persists in the schema and is reusable; a CTE exists only within one query
items.explain: A view is a persistent, reusable schema object; a CTE is local to a single statement. Neither stores data, but only the view survives the query.

items.q: Changes made through a valid (single-table) updatable view are:
options: Reflected in the underlying base table
items.explain: Because a view has no data of its own, an insert/update/delete through an updatable view modifies the base table itself.

items.q: A role in SQL is best described as:
options: A named group of privileges that users inherit when granted the role
items.explain: A role bundles privileges under a name; granting the role to users gives them all its privileges, simplifying bulk permission management. Roles can be nested.

items.q: In `GRANT SELECT ON school.* TO 'bob'@'localhost'`, what does `school.*` specify?
options: All tables in the school database
items.explain: Scope db.* means all tables in that database. *.* = all databases/tables; db.table = one specific table.

items.q: Which privilege allows a user to grant privileges to other users?
items.explain: GRANT OPTION is the administrative privilege that lets a recipient pass privileges on to others.

items.q: A trigger is defined by which three components?
items.explain: The event-condition-action (ECA) model: an event (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) checks the trigger, a condition must hold, and then the action executes.

items.q: In a row-level trigger, what do NEW and OLD refer to?
options: NEW = the inserted/updated row's values; OLD = the deleted/pre-update row's values
items.explain: NEW holds the values of the row being inserted/updated; OLD holds the prior values for an updated/deleted row. FOR EACH ROW runs the body per affected row.

items.q: To validate and reject invalid data before it is stored, which trigger timing is appropriate?
items.explain: A BEFORE trigger runs before the modification, so it can validate (e.g. SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000') and prevent a bad row from ever being inserted.

items.q: Why might a CheckMarks BEFORE INSERT trigger that rejects marks <0 or >100 still allow a NULL marks value?
options: NULL < 0 and NULL > 100 both evaluate to UNKNOWN, so the IF condition is not TRUE
The trigger has a bug in syntax
items.explain: Three-valued logic: comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN, so neither condition is TRUE and no error is signalled — the NULL row passes through.

items.q: A key distinction between a function and a stored procedure is:
options: A function must return a value and is used inside an expression; a procedure is CALLed and need not return anything
items.explain: Functions return exactly one value (or table) and appear in expressions; procedures are invoked with CALL, support IN/OUT/INOUT parameters, and need not return a value.

items.q: Which procedure parameter mode passes a value in, lets the procedure modify it, and returns the new value?
items.explain: INOUT combines IN and OUT: the caller supplies a value, the procedure changes it, and the updated value is returned. IN is input-only (default); OUT is output-only.

items.q: A MySQL function is DETERMINISTIC when:
options: It always returns the same result for the same inputs (and functions are NON-deterministic by default)
items.explain: DETERMINISTIC means identical inputs always yield identical outputs; it must be declared explicitly because functions are NON-DETERMINISTIC by default.

items.q: How is a stored procedure invoked?
options: By referencing it in a SELECT list
items.explain: Procedures are run with CALL procedure_name(args). They can also be invoked from triggers, other procedures, or applications — but not used inside an expression like a function.

items.q: How do window functions differ from GROUP BY aggregates?
options: They compute across a window of rows WITHOUT collapsing them — every input row is retained
They only work on one column
items.explain: GROUP BY collapses each group to one row; a window function keeps every row and attaches the computed value, so you can show a value and its group average side by side.

items.q: After two rows tie for rank 1, what rank does the next row get under RANK() vs DENSE_RANK()?
items.explain: RANK() skips after ties → the next rank is 3 (gap). DENSE_RANK() leaves no gap → the next rank is 2.

items.q: Which window function assigns a unique sequential number to every row with no ties?
items.explain: ROW_NUMBER() numbers rows 1,2,3,... uniquely, breaking ties arbitrarily. RANK/DENSE_RANK give equal values the same rank.

items.q: The LAG() window function returns:
options: The previous row's value within the ordered partition
items.explain: LAG(col, offset, default) returns the value from a preceding row; LEAD does the same for following rows. Useful for comparing a row to its neighbour.

items.q: Why can't you put a window function directly in a WHERE clause?
options: Syntax forbids any function in WHERE
Window functions are evaluated after WHERE; to filter on one, wrap the query and filter in an outer query/CTE
items.explain: Windowing happens after FROM/WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING, so a window result isn't available to WHERE. Compute it in a subquery/CTE, then filter outside (e.g. top-N).

items.q: What must be created before using MATCH(...) AGAINST(...) for full-text search?
options: A FULLTEXT index on the searched columns
items.explain: FTS requires a FULLTEXT index on the column(s); the columns inside MATCH() must match those covered by the index.

items.q: In Boolean-mode full-text search, what do the `+` and `-` operators mean?
options: +word = word must be present; -word = word must not be present
items.explain: In BOOLEAN MODE: + requires a word, - excludes it, "..." is an exact phrase, and * is a prefix wildcard.

items.q: Compared with LIKE/REGEXP, a major advantage of full-text search is:
options: It uses an index and ranks results by relevance with accurate word-boundary detection
items.explain: FTS uses a full-text index (fast), ranks by relevance, detects word boundaries (so 'cat' won't match 'concatenate'), and supports boolean/phrase queries — none of which LIKE does well.

items.q: Which full-text search mode is the default and ignores stopwords like 'a' and 'the'?
items.explain: Natural Language Mode is the default; it returns a relevance score and ignores common stopwords. Boolean Mode adds operators; Query Expansion broadens the search using top matches.

items.q: What does WITH CHECK OPTION do on an updatable view defined with a WHERE filter?
options: Rejects any insert/update through the view that would violate the view's WHERE condition
items.explain: WITH CHECK OPTION forbids inserting/updating rows that fall outside the view's defining condition (which would otherwise enter the base table but vanish from the view). CASCADED also enforces underlying views' conditions.

items.q: 'Find employees earning more than the average salary of THEIR OWN department' is written with `WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department_id = outer.department_id)`. This is a:
options: Correlated subquery (re-evaluated once per outer row)
items.explain: Because the subquery references outer.department_id, it must be recomputed for each employee using that employee's department — a correlated subquery. A plain subquery (no outer reference) would run only once.

items.q: How does a plain (nested) subquery differ from a correlated subquery in execution?
options: A plain subquery is independent and runs once; a correlated subquery references the outer row and runs once per candidate row
A correlated subquery runs once; a plain one runs per row
items.explain: A plain subquery is evaluated a single time and its value feeds the outer query. A correlated subquery depends on each outer row, so it executes repeatedly — which can make it slow.

items.q: In a `BEFORE INSERT ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger, what does `SET NEW.salary = 25000` accomplish?
options: It rewrites the value that will actually be stored for that row
items.explain: A BEFORE trigger can modify NEW, so the stored value is changed (here, capping/resetting the salary). Only BEFORE triggers can rewrite NEW; by AFTER the row is already written.

items.q: In a recursive CTE building an org chart from employee(ssn, superssn), what identifies the anchor (base) rows, and why must UNION ALL be used?
options: superssn IS NULL marks the root(s); UNION ALL is required because plain UNION would de-duplicate and break the recursion
The highest ssn; either UNION works
items.explain: Employees with superssn IS NULL are the roots (anchor). Each recursive step finds subordinates (e.superssn = OH.ssn). UNION ALL (not UNION) is mandatory so rows aren't removed during iteration.
